slides.title: McCulloh-Pitts (MP) Neurons
slides.text:
McCulloh-Pitts (MP) Neurons
•  Warren McCulloh (neuroscientist) and Walter Pitts (logician)          𝒚𝝐{𝟎, 𝟏}
   introduced artificial neurons in 1943.
•   It can only predict two states – on or off.                                               f
•  Consists of 2 parts:                                                                         g
    –  g that aggregates the inputs (here, 𝑥1, 𝑥2, 𝑥3): 𝒈𝒙= 𝜮𝒊=𝟏𝒏  𝒙𝒊
    –   f takes a decision based on the aggregation to give the output y: 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑔(𝑥))
•  𝜃 is the threshold parameter (decided by the user) to which       𝒙𝟏  𝒙𝟐  𝒙𝟑
  we compare the aggregated output for decision-making.
•  Path: Input -> aggregation ≥𝜃 -> output
              𝑦= 𝑓(𝑔𝑥) = 1 𝑖𝑓 𝑔(𝑥) ≥ 𝜃
                       = 0 𝑖𝑓  𝑔(𝑥) < 𝜃
•  Both inputs & outputs are either 0/1.

                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: 1943 McCulloh/Pitts historical attribution; binary input/output. Diagram bottom x1,x2,x3→aggregation g→decision f→y. g=sum xi, manually chosen threshold theta, y=1 when g>=theta including equality, else0. This simplified non-inhibitory unit-weight model is not all historical variants.

slides.text:
MP Neurons

•  This representation means for inputs 𝑥1, 𝑥2, 𝑥3, . . 𝑥𝑛if the sum g(x) ≥𝜃 , the
   neuron will fire (𝒚= 𝟏), else it won’t.
•  Output 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑔(𝑥))
•  Example: Is the patient fine?
    –  𝑥1: is Looking Fine
    –  𝑥2: has Normal Voice
    –  𝑥3: have Confirmed Verbally
    – 𝑦= 1 → Patient is fine
    – 𝑦= 0 → Patient is unwell
    –  Note: 𝑥𝑖, 𝑦 𝜖 {0,1}

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text:
Limitations
 •   It cannot process real-valued inputs; hence, it cannot solve non-linearly
    separable problems.
    –  It classifies all the inputs that produce an output of 1 as, say, Class A, & the ones
         that give an output of 0 would belong to, say, Class B.
 •  No learning or adaptation mechanism.
    – No training mechanism involved, acts more like a logic gate.

 •  Solution: The classical perceptron model, invented by Frank Rosenblatt
    in 1958.
 • A much refined version would be the perceptron model
   invented by Minsky and Papert in 1969.
 • We shall discuss this refined version.




                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Printed inference cannot process real-valued inputs; hence cannot solve nonlinearly separable problems is misleading: binary XOR already nonseparable, and accepting real inputs does not remove a single affine-threshold boundary. Claims no learning in MP, Rosenblatt1958 perceptron, then a refined perceptron invented by Minsky/Papert1969; verify historical attribution and do not treat their1969 analysis as an invented learning model without support.

slides.title: The perceptron model
slides.text:
The perceptron model
•   It is the foundational building block of modern
   Deep Learning.
•   It consists of:
    –  Inputs (𝒙𝟏, 𝒙𝟐, … , 𝒙𝟑).
    – Weights (𝒘𝟏, 𝒘𝟐, … , 𝒘𝟑): learnable parameters that
      determine the importance of each input.
    –  Bias(𝒘𝟎).
    –  Activation function: Similar to the MP Neuron, an
       aggregation function that calculates the weighted sum will
       be passed through a mathematical filter (activation
        function) before giving the final decision output (𝒚)
         𝑦= 1 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=0𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖≥0
                               0          = 0 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=0𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖<




                                                                                                           9

visualInspection.notes: Learnable weights plus bias w0; diagram x0=1,w0=-theta and x1–x3 with w1–w3 enter step node, y exits. Formula sum i=0..n wi xi >=0 fires, <0 off. Bullet lists x1,x2,...x3 and w1,w2,...w3 despite general n, so distinguish illustrated three inputs from arbitrary n. Bias is included exactly once.

slides.title: The concept of bias
slides.text:
The concept of bias
•  How did 𝑤0 become the bias?
•  The original equation is:  𝑦= 1 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=1𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖≥𝜃
                                           𝜃                   = 0 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=1𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖<
      Isn’t 𝜃 decided by the user?
•  Setting a threshold is a manual approach that exists in the MP Neurons. So, we
   have to convert it into a learnable parameter like the weights via:
                                                 {Set 𝒙𝟎= 𝟏; Set 𝒘𝟎= −𝜽}         𝑦= 1 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=1𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖−𝜃≥0
                                   0  {Set 𝒙𝟎= 𝟏 ;Set 𝒘𝟎= −𝜽}           = 0 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=1𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖−𝜃<
  ⇒         𝑦 = 1 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=0𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖≥0
                                  0            = 0 𝑖𝑓   Σ𝑖=0𝑛𝑤𝑖∗𝑥𝑖<
•  Now, bias is also a learnable parameter like the weights
•  Since 𝒙𝟎= 𝟏 is fixed, bias is not scaled like weights & it
   solely determines the shift.



                                                                                                           10

visualInspection.notes: Derivation moves theta to left and sets x0=1,w0=-theta, allowing sum from0 and threshold0. Bias is learned; fixed constant input means its contribution does not scale with a measured feature. Last statement solely determines shift should be scoped with other weights fixed; boundary offset depends on w normalization as well.

slides.title: Perceptron Learning Algorithm
slides.text:
Perceptron Learning Algorithm

•  Suppose we have 2 classes of inputs to classify:
   – 𝑐𝑙𝑎𝑠𝑠 𝑃 →𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡𝑠 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ 𝑙𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙 1
   – 𝑐𝑙𝑎𝑠𝑠 𝑁 →𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡𝑠 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ 𝑙𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙 0
•  We’ll assume they’re linearly separable and the perceptron must be able to
   learn how to make this decision.
•  The aim of this algorithm is to find that set of weights (𝑤0, 𝑤1, … 𝑤𝑛) that
   makes this possible.
•    If the prediction is correct, the weights remain
  unchanged.





                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: P label1,N label0; explicit linear-separability assumption; seek weights w0..wn; correct classification leaves parameters unchanged. The next page main prose discusses positive errors, but its actual pseudocode inset includes both positive and negative updates. Convergence depends on the full algorithm and stated separability.

slides.title: Perceptron Learning Algorithm
slides.text:
Perceptron Learning Algorithm
•  Step 1: Initialise weights & biases
   –  Usually, initialised to random small numbers
•  Step 2: Pick a random point 𝒙∈𝑃 𝑈 𝑁
•  Step 3: Measure the dot product
   ➢𝒘. 𝒙= ‖𝐰‖‖𝐱‖𝐜𝐨𝐬 𝜶
•  Step 4: If 𝒘. 𝒙 is negative for 𝑥∈𝑃,⇒𝛼> 90°
  ⇒ misclassification has occurred
   –  This means the current weights are wrong
•  Step 5: Update the current weight 𝒘𝒏𝒆𝒘= 𝒘+ 𝒙
   – The extra addition will increase the current weight which
         will yield a positive dot product.
•  Step 6: Repeat until all inputs are classified correctly



                                                                                                           13

visualInspection.notes: Actual pseudocode inset contains BOTH updates: positive example with w·x<0 adds x; negative example with w·x>=0 subtracts x. Thus equality is correctly positive. Inset explicitly samples P union N until convergence. Main prose discusses only positive errors, and falsely suggests one addition yields a positive dot product. It increases the dot product by ||x||² but may remain negative; adding x also need not increase every weight component. Angle formula needs nonzero vectors. Treat bias consistently through explicit augmented input.

•  The problem is that it is a binary switch – step function
•  The step function is a hard activation that works well for a simple perceptron.

slides.title: Vanishing Gradient Problem
slides.text:
Vanishing Gradient Problem & its solution
•  During Backpropagation (upcoming), gradients are multiplied layer by layer from
   the output back to the input.
•  The Core Issue: If we use Sigmoid or Tanh, the maximum gradient is small (e.g.,
  max gradient of Sigmoid is 0.25).
•  The Chain Effect: Multiplying many small numbers (say, 0.25*0.25*0.25…) causes
   the gradient to vanish or shrink to nearly zero as it reaches the earlier layers.
•  Impact on Robotics: The robot brain stops learning in its initial layers, meaning
     it cannot extract fundamental features from sensors
    effectively.
•  Solutions: ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit), Leaky ReLU,
  GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit)




                                                                                                          16

visualInspection.notes: Products of small gradients can attenuate early-layer signal. Printed shared example max derivative0.25 is sigmoid-specific: tanh maximum is1. Weight Jacobians also matter, so multiplying only activation maxima does not prove every network vanishes. ReLU, LeakyReLU and GELU can mitigate but do not universally eliminate gradient pathologies.

slides.title: Anatomy of a Neural Network
slides.text:
Architecture of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)
•  Neural Networks are made of:
    –  Input layer
           • Each neuron/node in this layer corresponds
         to an input feature.
    – Hidden layer                                                        (𝟐)
           • An MLP can have a single (shallow neural
        network) or multiple(deep neural network) no. of hidden layers.   (𝟏)
           • Each neuron in this layer processes the information
         received from the input layer via an activation function.
           • For example, the activation happening in the first neuron
          of the hidden layer (1) using ReLU can be represented as:
                             𝑎(1) = ReLU(𝑾(𝟏)𝒙+ 𝑏(1))


                                                                                                           18

visualInspection.notes: Fully connected diagram has3 input nodes,4 hidden nodes,1 output:16 edge weights and5 biases if each noninput neuron has one,21 totalparameters. One hidden layer called shallow, multiple deep. Equation a^(1)=ReLU(W^(1)x+b^(1)) is vector layer output with W1 shape4x3,b1 shape4x1. Prose first-neuron wording requires a row/scalar version, not the whole layer matrix.

slides.title: Architecture of a Multi-Layer Perceptron
slides.text:
Architecture of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)

    – Output layer
           • The output layer generates the final prediction or result.
           • The number of neurons = the number of outputs.
           • For example, an output layer (2) using Sigmoid activation will look like:
                            ypred = Sigmoid(𝑾(𝟐)𝒂(𝟏) + 𝑏(2))
•  Note: Activation functions are used in hidden layers to learn complex patterns
    (e.g., ReLU,tanh), and in the output layer to format the final prediction
    (e.g., Sigmoid for Binary, Softmax for Multi-class).

slides.title: Forward Pass
slides.text:
Forward Pass
•  Data flows from the input layer to the output layer via hidden layers.
•  Forward propagation has the following steps:
    – Each neuron computes a weighted sum
                + 𝑏           • 𝑧= 𝜮𝒊=𝟏𝒏  (𝒘𝒊. 𝒙𝒊)
         (Note: From here, bias will be represented as b, instead of 𝑤0)
    – The weighted sum 𝑧 is passed through an activation function
           • 𝑦= 𝑓(𝑧) where f could be Sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, Leaky ReLU, etc.
•  No learning happens in forward propagation.
•  This is the phase where the output will be predicted.





                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: Explicit sum i1..n wi xi+b; bias notation switches from w0 to b. z then activation y=f(z). Forward pass alone predicts, does not update learned weights in the stated feedforward training model. Include bias once and distinguish stored state from gradient update.

slides.title: Loss Functions
slides.text:
Loss Functions
•  Once the network generates an output, the next step is to calculate the loss
   using a loss function.
•   It guides the learning process by measuring the quality of the prediction by
   comparing the predicted output to the actual label.
•   It is used during training only.
• We use different loss functions for classification and regression problems.
•  Common Loss Functions are:
   – Cross-Entropy Loss for classification Problems
        (both binary & multi-class)
   – Mean Squared Error (MSE) for Regression Problems





                                                                                                          22

visualInspection.notes: Loss compares predicted output to actual labels, common cross-entropy for classification and MSE regression. Printed used during training only is false if labelled validation/test loss is computed without updates; ordinary unlabelled inference need not compute supervised loss.

slides.title: Back Propagation
slides.text:
Back Propagation
•  The goal of training an MLP is to minimize the loss function by adjusting the
   network's weights and biases, achieved through back propagation.
•   It is achieved through three key steps:
•  Step 1: Gradient Calculation
   – Calculate gradients of the loss function w.r.t. weights & bias
•  Step 2: Error Propagation
   – The error is propagated backwards through the network, layer by layer.
•  Step 3: Gradient Descent
   – The network updates the weights & biases by moving to the
    opposite direction of the gradient
    –  We’ll discuss in detail in the upcoming slides.




                                                                                                          24

visualInspection.notes: Training adjusts weights/biases to minimize loss. Lists gradient calculation, backward error propagation, gradient descent opposite gradient. Distinguish chain-rule gradient computation (backprop) from chosen optimizer update; neither alone implies global minimum.

Example
•  Problem: A robot operating in a cluttered environment must avoid collisions by
   using proximity sensor readings (𝑥) to determine the braking torque (𝑦𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑​)
   required to stop its movement.
•  The Data: For the given data point, when the proximity sensor detects an object
   at a distance of 2 m, the desired braking torque is 10 Nm to prevent the robot
   from moving toward a potential collision. Thus, 𝑥 = 2, 𝑦𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒= 10.
•   Initial Brain State: Initialize the weights randomly.
    –  Let's say Weight 𝑤= 3.0 and Bias 𝑏= 1.0.
    –  Learning Rate 𝜂= 0.1

One distance/torque pair cannot identify a unique affine map or prove safety/generalization.

•  Transformers: The Reasoning Engine

        simultaneously, regardless of their order.
    –  Robotics Application: The backbone of modern Vision-
       Language-Action (VLA) models in Embodied AI, allowing
       robots to understand complex human commands (e.g.,
        pick up the red block next to the cup) and map them
         directly to motor actions.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary
•   Neural Networks (ANNs) are inspired by biological neurons.
•  They have evolved from simple logic-based McCulloh-Pitts models to trainable Perceptrons
    that use learnable weights and biases.
•   Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are structured with input, hidden, and output layers.
•  They apply activation functions like ReLU and GELU to learn complex patterns.
•  Networks learn through a continuous cycle of a forward pass for prediction, loss calculation
    for evaluation, backpropagation to calculate error gradients & gradient descent to update
   parameters.
•  Specialized models handle different data types: CNNs act as eyes
   for spatial grids, RNNs act as memory for sequential data &
   Transformers serve as a reasoning engine.
•  These neural networks power real-world applications such as
   visual object detection, autonomous navigation & VLAs for
  Embodied AI.


                                                                                                          37
